name: Echinacea

authorship.writtenFor: rnawiki beginner readers who want to know what echinacea is and what it might do
authorship.method: Facts taken from public-domain U.S. government sources listed below. Every sentence here was written from scratch for rnawiki. No source sentence, table, list order, or heading set was reused.
authorship.limits: Reference content only. It reports what a government health page and drug labels recorded. It gives no dosing, no diagnosis, and no treatment advice.

identity.latinName: Echinacea purpurea, Echinacea angustifolia, Echinacea pallida
identity.whatItIs: A group of perennial plants from North America, sold mainly as dietary supplements for colds and other respiratory infections.

oneLineAnswer: Echinacea is a North American plant sold for colds. It may slightly lower your chance of catching one.
whatItDoes: Echinacea is not one plant. The name covers several perennials related to daisies and ragweed.
Native Americans used Echinacea purpurea for breathing infections, tooth pain, and snakebite.
Products sold today mostly aim at the common cold and other respiratory infections.
Sellers base that use on the idea that some echinacea species may stimulate the immune system.
NCCIH, a US government health agency, reports that taking echinacea may slightly lower your chance of catching a cold.
whatWeDoNotKnow: NCCIH says it is still unclear whether echinacea shortens a cold you already have.
It is unclear whether echinacea helps other conditions, including eczema.
One study suggested children taking echinacea had fewer respiratory infections and complications. NCCIH says that is not enough evidence for a clear connection.
NCCIH-funded research found that soil conditions change the plant's bacterial community, and that this changes how echinacea extracts behave.
No fetched source names which species, plant part, or preparation works best, or shows any of them clearly works.
Little is known about whether echinacea is safe while breastfeeding.
Whether echinacea changes how the body handles medicines broken down by the liver is disputed. Interactions with immunosuppressants or caffeine are only suspected.
safetyNotes: NCCIH says echinacea extracts of E. purpurea, and some E. purpurea with E. angustifolia mixtures, are likely safe for most adults for short periods.
Some people have allergic reactions to echinacea, and NCCIH says those reactions can be severe.
An FDA drug label warns against echinacea if you are allergic to other daisy family plants, called Compositae.
The side effects reported most often are gut symptoms: belly pain, nausea, or stomach pain.
NCCIH says E. purpurea extract is possibly safe for children for short periods. In one trial, some children developed rashes that may have been allergic reactions.
For pregnancy, NCCIH reports some studies where extracts were possibly safe for up to 7 days in the first trimester. Safety while breastfeeding is largely unknown.
NCCIH says evidence about interactions with liver-processed drugs conflicts, and calls interactions with immunosuppressants or caffeine theoretical.
In the US, supplements are not approved by the FDA before sale, and supplement rules are looser than drug rules.
Homeopathic products that list echinacea say their uses come from traditional practice and were not FDA evaluated.
NCCIH says to talk with a child's health care provider before giving a child an echinacea product.
confidenceRationale: The plant description, the cold findings, and most of the safety picture come from one fetched source, the NCCIH Echinacea page, which is a US federal publication in the public domain. An independent FDA drug label fetched through openFDA supports the daisy-family allergy caution, and a DailyMed listing shows echinacea sits in ordinary cough and throat products. No second fetched source covers the botanical or cold-outcome claims, so confidence is medium rather than high.
gaps: No second fetched source covers the botanical claims (species, range, daisy-family relation) or the cold-outcome claims; those rest on the NCCIH page alone.

The NCCIH page would not load through a plain text fetch, which returned stylesheet code instead of the article. Its text was read from the rendered page, and each quote used here was checked against that rendered text.
NCCIH's at-a-glance subpage returned a 404 and was not used.
PubChem has no compound record for echinacea. Name and substance lookups returned 404, and the compound page is script-rendered, so only the autocomplete term Echinacoside Ethanolate could be read.
MedlinePlus has no echinacea page (404), and its Common Cold health topic does not mention echinacea.

The DailyMed label-detail request returned HTTP 415. The echinacea labels found there and in openFDA are homeopathic or multi-ingredient products, so they document how echinacea is marketed rather than whether it works.
No fetched source gives trial outcome numbers or effect sizes, so this page reports only whether a finding was called unclear, slight, or unsupported.
The fetched NCCIH page does not say which plant parts are used, so the identity block records no partsUsed value.
Nothing here covers dosing on purpose. Product labels state doses, but this page reports no amount to take.
MedlinePlus drug monographs and herb monographs were deliberately not fetched or cited, because NLM licenses that content.

evidence.claim: Echinacea is a group of species, including Echinacea purpurea, Echinacea angustifolia, and Echinacea pallida.
evidence.quote: Latin Names: Echinacea purpurea, Echinacea angustifolia, Echinacea pallida
evidence.source: NCCIH, Echinacea: Usefulness and Safety (public domain, last updated November 2024)

evidence.claim: Echinacea also goes by purple coneflower, coneflower, and American coneflower.
evidence.quote: Common Names: echinacea, purple coneflower, coneflower, American coneflower
evidence.source: NCCIH, Echinacea: Usefulness and Safety (public domain)

evidence.claim: Echinacea plants are perennials in the same plant family as sunflowers, daisies, and ragweed.
evidence.quote: Echinacea species are perennials that are closely related to sunflowers, daisies, and ragweed.
evidence.source: NCCIH, Echinacea: Usefulness and Safety (public domain)

evidence.claim: Echinacea is native to the area east of the Rocky Mountains in the United States, though it is widely grown elsewhere today.
evidence.quote: echinacea species are native to areas east of the Rocky Mountains in the United States
evidence.source: NCCIH, Echinacea: Usefulness and Safety (public domain)

evidence.claim: Native Americans used Echinacea purpurea as a medicine for respiratory tract infections, tooth pain, and snakebite.
